Application monitoring isn't quite the role of a firewall, as Linux has a half dozen means to have an application eventually talk to a network. Internet socket, file socket, emulate a network card, stream though a serial link, directly talk to the print or email server, probably some more...

However there is infrastructure for monitoring applications, SELinux, AppArmor, grsecurity and several others do application monitoring. They all monitor all actions an application does, blocking one that it shouldn't. There are not quite easy means of setting up most of these, however they do all have a rather large community with cut-n-paste examples available.
Yea, I use apparmour currently. It's a bit of work but like you say I found the online rulesets and that made it easier.

The end result for any Linux firewall should be to have the kernel eventually do as much work as possible. Access from network card to kernel and back should run at line speed for any semi-modern machine. The end results for anything should be the same, the same kernel used in all of Linux should be doing as much work as possible.

I've run Shorewall for years. It's not quite easy to set up, or overly well designed, but comes with some great examples and community. It's started as a script to compensate for some incompatibilities in Linux native firewall years ago. The original issue hasn't been one for a decade, however Shorewall still see regular updates. Shorewall merely checks for typos add some organization before handing off a set of rules for the kernel.
